title: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's letters
hookLine: the just caliph's letters to governors about fairness and restraint
tomorrow: what does a good leader have in common with a shepherd?

cards: Some emails get rewritten again and again, and the angry version never leaves the outbox. Others go out in one hot minute, and can't be unsent. Can an email be fair?
Can a ruler's orders be? Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, a caliph remembered for justice, wrote to his governors, and the letters later writers kept keep coming back to fairness.

teach.b: One governor, the story goes, wrote asking for money to build a wall around his city. Umar wrote back: fortify it with justice, and clear its roads of oppression.

To another he wrote: if your power over people tempts you to wrong them, remember God's power over you. That's the word for today, lightly: fairness in writing, a ruler using his pen to keep power gentle.

teach.h: A WEEK OF LINES, HELD UP.
teach.b: Six lines, held up together. Zayn al-Abidin asked to be good to my neighbors. His prayer for noble character answered every wrong with better: the noblest character.
The farewell sermon said we're all from Adam. Abu Bakr opened his rule with correct me. Umar's letter told a judge: equal before you.
Ali told a governor that every stranger is equal in creation. Different voices: a prayer, a sermon, a speech, three letters. Look at the thread.
Every one of these came from someone with some power, over a household, a pulpit, a court, a province, and every one turns that power toward the people with less.
This was a week of words from the top, and all of them point down, with care.

how: Muslims tell stories of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's letters in sermons and classes on justice; the lines about fortifying a city with justice and remembering God's power are among the ones retold.

games.q: what does “umar ibn abd al-aziz's letters” mean?
o: a caliph's poems about his love of the desert
a caliph's rules for building mosques and walls
a just caliph's letters telling governors to be fair

games.q: the letters, and the week — tap the pairs.

s: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told a governor to build a higher wall
the story says: fortify it with justice.
he reminded a governor of God's power over him
if your power tempts you to wrong people, remember God's.
this week's lines all came from people with no power
each came from someone with some power, turning it toward people with less.

games.q: you're writing the house rules for the family group chat. what fits this week's letters?
o: write them so the youngest would call them fair.
write them so nobody can argue with the parents.
skip rules; fairness means nobody's in charge.
games.why: the week's letters turn power toward the ones with less: fair enough that the weakest would say so.

practice: Open a message you've been meaning to send, one with some heat in it, or write one now. Read it once as the person receiving it.
Change one line so it would still be fair if they showed it to everyone, and keep it as a version for now.

wordCard.voice: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's letters: a caliph's letters to his governors, using the pen to keep power fair.

orig.note: Arabic: al-'adl, justice, the word behind 'fortify it with justice'.

carryVoice: That's a week: fairness in writing, the pen turned toward the people with less. Week done.
